Hamnet author Maggie O'Farrell on maps as rebellion

2026-07-29 William O'Connor (National Geographic) cartography, mapmaking, Ireland, Ordnance Survey, Maggie O'Farrell, Land, literature, cultural mapping
Read the source article

Quick summary

Bestselling author Maggie O'Farrell discusses her novel Land and the artistry of mapmaking, exploring how the Ordnance Survey of Ireland became both an instrument of colonial control and a devastating record of pre-famine Ireland.

Key takeaways

  • Maggie O'Farrell's novel Land revolves around mapmaking in Ireland, centered on the Ordnance Survey of Ireland (1825-1846)—once the world's largest mapmaking endeavor.
  • The Ordnance Survey was originally launched by the British for taxation purposes but became a devastating record of pre- and post-famine Ireland.
  • O'Farrell describes mapmaking as a "peculiar mix of science and storytelling, mathematics and artistry."
  • The novel tells the story of an unnamed Irish peninsula across thousands of years through the family of a mapmaker.
  • By 1852, just six years after the Survey's completion, a million people had died and nearly two million had emigrated during the Great Famine.
